content: A somatic cell refers to any cell that constitutes the body of an organism. The term somatic originates from the Greek word sōma (σῶμα), which translates to body. Somatic cells, by definition, are distinct from germline cells. In mammals, germline cells include spermatozoa and ova (commonly referred to as gametes), which combine during fertilization to form a zygote. This zygote is the single cell from which the entire mammalian embryo develops. All other cell types in the mammalian body, excluding sperm, ova, the precursor cells that produce them (gametocytes), and undifferentiated stem cells, are classified as somatic cells. These include the cells that make up internal organs, skin, bones, blood, and connective tissues. Somatic cells can be simply defined as non-sex cells, though this is a broad and not always precise description. In humans, somatic cells contain 46 chromosomes, organized into 23 pairs. Each pair consists of one chromosome inherited from the father and one from the mother. Human somatic cells have twice the number of chromosomes as germline cells (sex cells). Germline cells contain only 23 chromosomes. During conception, germline cells fuse to form a zygote, which restores the chromosome number to 46. The sex of the resulting offspring is determined by the specific sex chromosome (X or Y) contributed by the germline cells. In humans and other species with somatic cells that have chromosomes arranged in pairs, these organisms are referred to as diploid. Their germline cells, which contain single, unpaired chromosomes, are termed haploid. However, in many other species, the arrangement of chromosomes in somatic cells can be more complex. Some species organize their somatic cell chromosomes in sets of four (tetraploid) or even six (hexaploid). This means that their germline cells can be diploid or even triploid. For example, a hexaploid species has somatic cells containing six copies of each chromosome.
